zones.label: Column 1

Supplied page subset consulted for lexical identification, not as a substitute transcription. lines.note: Gebon denotes a low grade or inferior thing; the example continues into gexō on the next row. The scan supports Guebon and the divided gue-, rather than OCR Guebem and guc-.
Completes gebon gexō no hito, a person of low standing or character. The Portuguese calls him a man of low rank; the nasal abbreviation in Homẽ is retained without expansion.

runs.text: Grao inferior em comparação de Chǔbon, &

lines.note: The second sense is an inferior grade relative to chūbon and jōbon. The marked u in Chǔbon has a caron, not a tilde; this Japanese comparison occurs inside the Portuguese explanation.
Jōbon completes the comparison of lower, middle and upper grades. This is Japanese vocabulary embedded in the preceding Portuguese sentence, not a separate headword.

runs.text: Terceira parte, ou vltima de tres li-

lines.note: Gebu is the third or last division in a three-volume work. The printed li- begins livros on the next physical row.
Completes livros, ou volumes: books or volumes. This short continuation belongs to Gebu and remains a separate line.
Gekaku is explained by kiba and tsuno, tusk and horn. The Portuguese begins the example of a wild boar; por continues into co without adding an unprinted hyphen.
Completes porco montes and compares the tusk with that of a boar or elephant, then adds horn. The historical spelling montes is retained without supplying an accent.
Gekai is this lower world; the gloss inferior describes its position, without adding a modern cosmological identification.

runs.text: Os derradeiros dez dias do mes em cõ

lines.note: Gekan denotes the final ten days of the month. The abbreviated cõ begins comparação across the physical break.

runs.text: paração de Chǔcan. jǒcan. Que ſão os dez do

lines.note: The comparison names chūkan and jōkan, the middle and first ten-day periods. The scan supports marked vowels and the capital Ch; the separators are retained as printed rather than normalized into a list.
Completes the explanation: the ten days in the middle and those at the beginning. This belongs to the comparison under Guecan.
Gechaku is paraphrased by kudari-tsuku, arriving after coming down. The following Portuguese identifies the point of departure.

runs.text: Miyaco, ou de outra parte ſuperior.

lines.note: The arrival is from Miyako or another superior place. Miyaco is a Japanese place designation within the Portuguese sentence and remains in the locally printed italic type.
Gechi, glossed shita no chie, means limited knowledge or understanding. The Portuguese is Pouco saber, not OCR Fouco; the example follows.
Gekon gechi na hito describes a person of weak ability and little understanding. The Portuguese sa continues into ber below without a supplied hyphen.
Completes saber and adds weak ability. The two Portuguese characteristics explain gechi and gekon together, rather than introducing another entry.
Geko denotes someone who does not drink wine or alcoholic drink. The scan supports Peßoa rather than OCR Peßca; Gue- begins the following example.
Completes geko shō na hito, a non-drinking person. The Portuguese repeats the abstention and continues with additional qualities below.

runs.text: & no de mais he temperado, modesto, & apri

lines.note: The person is also temperate, modest and refined in other respects. The original modest-type ligature is retained as modest, without a global st/ſt substitution.
Morado completes aprimorado, refined or well-mannered. This single-word continuation finishes the description of the non-drinker.

Gekō is descending or going down, paraphrased kudari mukō. The initial is G, not OCR C, and both long-o marks are carons. Reinspection does not securely establish a word space inside the close printed Cudarimucǒ, so the baseline joining is retained.
The descent is especially from Miyako. The place name is embedded within the Portuguese explanation, rather than a Japanese synonym line.
Gekoku, kuni e kudaru, means returning from Miyako to one's own province or domain. The scan reads Guecocu, not Guccocu; Miya continues into co on the next row without an added hyphen.
Co completes Miyaco, and pera seu reino specifies return to one's own domain. The divided Japanese place name remains within the Portuguese sentence.
Gekokujō is paraphrased as the lower overcoming the upper. The Portuguese begins its social example with Sendo bai, continued as baixo below.

runs.text: xo, & criado, por ſuas boas partes, & induſ-

lines.note: Completes baixo: someone low-ranking and a servant rises through good qualities and industry. Xo is Portuguese, not Japanese, and is therefore included in the printed italic gloss.

runs.text: tria, ou fortuna vir a valer, & ſer ſenhor,

lines.note: Tria completes industria; fortune is given as another way the servant may gain standing and become a lord. The explanation continues the reversal of status.

runs.text: & o ſenhor vir a ſer criado, ou baixo.

lines.note: The former lord in turn becomes a servant or a low-ranking person. This completes the dictionary's explicit illustration of gekokujō.
Gekōdō, kudari mukō michi, is the path used in descending. Both marked o types in the headword remain carons; the Portuguese explanation follows.

runs.text: polo qual ſe dece de lugar alto, como quando

lines.note: The path leads down from a high place. The ensuing example makes clear that this can be the return route from worship or a visit.

runs.text: vem de viſitar o Cami, ou Fotoque.

lines.note: Completes the example of returning from visiting a kami or hotoke. The worn opening supports vem, not OCR vuem; Cami and Fotoque are Japanese religious terms embedded in Portuguese.
Gekon is explained as a person without kikon, stamina or perseverance. The printed Portuguese noun is Peßoa, not OCR Teßoa; its qualifying phrase continues below.

runs.text: fraca compreiſão, & q̃ não chega ao cabo nem

lines.note: Describes a weak constitution or capacity and failure to carry things through. The historical compreiſão and abbreviated q̃ are preserved, rather than modernized or expanded.
Completes the lack of perseverance, then contrasts jōkon, a person who possesses the opposite strength. The initial I in Iǒcon is the source's consonantal spelling.
Vigor and perseverance complete the description of jōkon. This is the contrasting positive term under Guecon, not an unrelated gloss.

runs.text: Nome de hũa dignidade, ou nobres

lines.note: Gekkei is described as a dignity or a class of nobles. The Portuguese number shift from a dignity to nobles is printed and has not been regularized.
The nobles serve the Dairi, the imperial court or sovereign referred to here. Dairi occurs within the Portuguese relative clause and is a typeface-review term.
Gekkyū is tsuki no miya, the moon palace. The u carries a caron in this impression; imagi- begins the Portuguese verb imaginão, not OCR irmagi-.

runs.text: não os gẽtios eſtar dentro da lũa onde hum como

lines.note: Completes imaginão: the dictionary reports a house imagined by non-Christians inside the moon. The worn initial n and the abbreviation in gẽtios support this reading; the analogy hum como continues below.
The dictionary likens the lunar inhabitant to an angel and says it makes the moon wax and wane. This reports the source's analogy, not an independent identification of the deity.
Gekkyūden is given the same moon-palace meaning as Guecqiǔ. The scan supports G and the ascender of d rather than OCR Cuecqiǔcen; the small u-mark is worn and is retained as a caron provisionally.
Gekka combines tsuki and hana, moon and flowers; the Portuguese uses lua and rosas. The printed nasal mark belongs to u in Lũa, not to an a.
Gedai is the title of a book. The example repeats Guedai- across the break; the initial G is supported by the visible type rather than OCR C.
Completes gedai wo kakitsukuru or osu, putting a title on a book. The object particle reads uo, not no, and the Portuguese verb Por replaces OCR Tor; nal- continues below.

runs.text: gum liuro, ou nas coſtas delle com outro papel

lines.note: The title may be placed on the book or on its back using another piece of paper. No sentence-final punctuation is supplied where the physical line continues.

runs.text: pegado ao modo de Iapão, ou da China.

lines.note: The paper is attached in the Japanese or Chinese manner. The scan resolves the garbled OCR as pegado ao modo de Iapão, ou da China; these geographical names are Portuguese forms, not Japanese typeface terms.
This homonymous gedai is equated with shitadai, a subordinate judicial official. The scan supplies iuſtiça and the worn final ou.
Completes the alternative description as a less senior governor. Gouernador is a single word; the OCR's internal gap and c are not supported.
Gedan, shita no dan, is a lower step or level. The line ends ou, introducing the synonymous inferior below.

runs.text: inferior. ¶ Item, Grao, ou laya de cou-

lines.note: After the literal lower step, a second sense concerns an inferior grade or class. The scan reads inferior, without OCR's extra t.
Completes cousa inferior and begins the sequence gedan, chūdan, jōdan: lower, middle and upper grades. The Japanese example is not an embedded Portuguese font-toggle term.
Jōdan completes the three-grade example. Its separate physical row is retained despite containing only the final term.
Gedat is Buddhist liberation, glossed to free or release. The checked final t is preserved; Bup. is a roman usage label, and O begins the following italic sentence.

runs.text: principal ſentido he liberdade a cerca das pai-

lines.note: The principal sense is freedom with respect to passions and vices. Pai- continues as paixões on the next row.
Xões completes paixões, followed by vices. This specifies the Buddhist liberation described under Guedat.
Geden is equated with zokusho, secular books concerning human affairs. The Portuguese hu- begins humanas across the line break.
Completes human and secular matters, then contrasts naiden, a book treating Buddhist subjects. The rightmost Liuro is worn but intelligible.

runs.text: que trata de couſas do Buppô.

lines.note: Completes naiden as a book about Buddhist teaching. The o in Buppô bears a circumflex, not the OCR grave; Buppô is embedded Japanese vocabulary.

Gedō is here glossed as doing harm or causing injury; gedō wo nasu continues below. On reinspection the V of Vt is unusually upright, so the provisional roman V and italic t are retained rather than regularizing the whole apparatus marker to italic.
Completes gedō wo nasu, then introduces an extended sense concerning ceremonies. Cerimoni- continues into as on the next row.

runs.text: as, ou deprecaçoẽs que fazem os feiticeiros, ou

lines.note: These ceremonies or supplications are performed by sorcerers or the group named on the following row. The unusual tilde placement in deprecaçoẽs is retained.

runs.text: Yamabuxis pera botar o diabo fora, ou pera ou

lines.note: Yamabushi are named as performers of rites to drive out the devil or for another purpose. The entire printed Portuguese-context line, including Yamabuxis, is italic; the isolated roman Y was an OCR styling error.
Tro completes outro, followed by effect or purpose. This closes the description of the rites under Guedǒ.
Gedoku is identified only as a particular medicine. The brief gloss does not establish an exact recipe or substance.
Gehai, shita no tomogara, denotes people of low or inferior rank. The Portuguese description continues on the next line.
The example gehai no hito repeats the same meaning. The scan supports Guefaino rather than OCR Cuefamno; Idẽ is a printed abbreviation of idem.
Gehit is redirected to the preferred kahit, shita no fude, inferior writing or workmanship. Meliùs is italic apparatus; Ru begins ruim without a supplied hyphen.

runs.text: im letra, ou ruim eſcriuão. Vt,

lines.note: Completes ruim letra and gives a poor writer as an alternative sense. The contrast begins jōhit, the superior counterpart; the checked final t remains unexpanded.

runs.text: Bom eſcriuão, ou pintor, & ruim eſ-

lines.note: Kahit completes the contrast with jōhit. The Portuguese explains a good writer or painter versus a poor one, and divides escriuão at the line ending.
Completes escriuão and repeats painter, finishing the comparison of good and poor workmanship. The line belongs to Guefit, not a new headword.

runs.text: Ma ley, ou ley do diabo, ſuperſtições,

lines.note: Gehō is described polemically as bad law, the devil's law, or superstitions. The scan reads ſuperſtições, not OCR ſuperſtiçães; the characterization belongs to the historical dictionary.
Gehō wo okonō means performing these practices. The example retains the circumflex on Guefô and the caron on voconǒ; es- continues into estas.
Completes these superstitions and ceremonies of the devil. This is the source's translation of the preceding example, not an added assessment.
Gehon is redirected to the preferred gebon, an inferior grade. Xitano xi- begins shita no shina and continues on the next row.
Na completes shina, grade or class; the Latin instruction means see above. The scan has na rather than OCR ria, agreeing with the Japanese paraphrase.
Gegu is explained as shita-jita no mono, people of inferior status. The G is visible despite wear; in continues into inferior below.
Ferior completes inferior, finishing the low-status-person definition. No new entry begins on this short continuation.
Gege is equated with zōri and described as footwear like sandals. The scan supports alparcas rather than alparras; the material is supplied next.
The sandals are made of straw, and gege is identified as women's vocabulary. The example begins with the same term.
Gege wo haku means putting on these straw sandals. The source retains haku as faqu in its romanization.
Gegyō, kudashi okonō, concerns a lord's giving or entrusting something for distribution. The recipient and administrative arrangement follow.

runs.text: ou entregar algũa couſa ao ſeu feitor, ou outros

lines.note: The lord hands something to his steward or other officials. The scan reads ao seu feitor, not OCR co; the tilde remains on u in algũa.

runs.text: officiaes pera ſe repartir, ou destribuir por ou-

lines.note: The officials are to apportion or distribute it among others. Historical destribuir is retained; ou- continues into outros.
Completes outros, then begins kono kome wa gegyō de gozaru: this rice is provided by the lord's order. Gozaru is divided across physical rows without an added mark.

runs.text: Eſte arroz manda dar o ſenhor, &c.

lines.note: Ru completes gozaru; the Portuguese says the lord orders this rice to be given. The translation confirms the distributive sense of Gueguiǒ.
Geji means an order or command. The example gives alternative verbs with geji wo, continuing onto the next line.
Nasu and kuwayuru complete the alternative constructions for giving a command. The Portuguese means to command or issue an order; Mãdar remains abbreviated.
Gejo, shimo onna, is glossed as an enslaved woman or a low-ranking female servant. This preserves the source's distinction rather than treating the two Portuguese alternatives as identical.
Completes the description as a woman of low-ranking service. The first tall letter in ſeruiço is long s, not OCR f.
Gejiki, yasui atai, is low value or a low price. The Portuguese and Japanese paraphrase agree on cheapness rather than moral baseness.
Ge-i is redirected to the preferred ka-i and means a low dignity or office. The internal hyphens are lexical and are not line-end divisions.
Baixo completes the description of a low-ranking dignity or post. This short continuation ends Gue-i.
Geiha is equated with toki no koe, a battle cry. The worn vowel in Toqino supports o in context; the Portuguese reads Grita, not OCR Gria.
Completes the cry given at the start of battle. The separate Guei at the far right is the catchword, not part of this definition; its duplicate has been removed from the body text.
